title: Statistical optimization of morphological analysis for various developed zeolitic imidazolate frameworks (ZIFs) using design of experiments
content: Zeolitic imidazolate frameworks (ZIFs) have attracted considerable attention owing to their high porosity, stability, and controllable physicochemical characteristics that can be used in drug delivery, gas separation, catalysis, and sensing, where particle size plays a critical role in determining performance. In this study, the design of experiment (DOE) approach based on response surface methodology (RSM) was used to optimize synthesis parameters of three types of zeolitic imidazolate frameworks, including ZIF-4, ZIF-11, and ZIF-67. Central composite design (CCD) was employed to examine the individual and combined influence of the concentration of metal precursors, ligands, and volume of solvent on the average particle size. Quadratic regression equations for each system were derived and validated via ANOVA. All three models were statistically significant (p ≤ 0.0001), with R2 values ranging from 0.9309 to 0.9793 and non-significant lack-of-fit tests (p > 0.05). Numerical optimization using the desirability function identified predicted optimal particle sizes of 114.754, 63.822, and 102.531 µm for ZIF-4, ZIF-11, and ZIF-67, respectively. Experimental validation yielded particle sizes of 123.54, 66.50, and 103.60 µm, corresponding to relative prediction errors of 7.11%, 4.03%, and 1.03%, respectively. The close agreement between the predicted and experimentally measured particle sizes supports the predictive capability of the developed models within the investigated experimental domains. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) analysis provided morphological and particle size characterization of the optimized samples, while X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis confirmed the characteristic crystalline structures of the synthesized ZIFs. Overall, the developed DOE-RSM framework provides a systematic approach for optimizing ZIF synthesis conditions and controlling particle size within the investigated experimental ranges.
